<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="2607:FB92:1F05:CB5D:2813:F9D2:CF1E:C285" /></noinclude><section begin="par44" />in Hebrew, also ''ûna'' (in the construct state ''û'') as the plural termination of masc. nouns in literary Arabic.

{{GHGmargin-letter|44|b}}
'''2.''' The characteristic {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}} of the second syllable becomes {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}} before an afformative beginning with a vowel, where it would otherwise stand in an open syllable (as {{GHGheb|text=קָֽטְלָ֫ה}}, {{GHGheb|text=קָֽטְל֫וּ}}; but in {{GHGterm|pause}} {{GHGheb|text=קָטָ֫לָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=קָטָ֫לוּ}}). Before an afformative beginning with a consonant the {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}} remains, whether in the tone-syllable ({{GHGheb|text=קָטַ֫לְתָּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=קָטַ֫לְתְּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=קָטַ֫לְתִּי}}, {{GHGheb|text=קָטַ֫לְנוּ}}; in {{GHGterm|pause}} {{GHGheb|text=קָטָ֫לְתָּ}} &c.) or ''before'' it. In the latter case, however, the {{GHGterm|Qameṣ}} of the first syllable, being no longer a pretonic vowel, becomes vocal {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}}; as {{GHGheb|text=קְטַלְתֶּ֫ם}}, {{GHGheb|text=קְטַלְתֶּ֫ן}}; cf. {{GHGpar|27|i}} and {{GHGpar|43|b}}. On the retention of ''ā'' with {{GHGterm|Metheg}} of the counter-tone in the ''Perf. consecutive'', cf. {{GHGpar|49|i}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|44|c}}
Rem. 1. Verbs ''middle ē'' in Hebrew (as in Ethiopic, but not in Arabic or Aramaic) generally change the ''E''-sound in their inflexion into {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}} (frequently so even in the 3rd sing. masc. Perf.). This tendency to assimilate to the more common verbs ''middle a'' may also be explained from the laws of vocalization of the tone-bearing closed penultima, which does not readily admit of {{GHGterm|Ṣere}}, and never of {{GHGterm|Ḥireq}}, of which the {{GHGterm|Ṣere}} is a lengthening (cf. {{GHGpar|26|p}}). On the other hand, {{GHGterm|Ṣere}} is retained in an open syllable; regularly so in the weak stems {{GHGheb|text=ל״א}} ({{GHGpar|74|g}}), before suffixes ({{GHGpar|59|i}}), and in the pausal forms of the strong stem in an open tone-syllable, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=דָּבֵ֫קָה|translate=it cleaveth}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=29|verse=10}} (not {{GHGheb|text=דָּבָ֫קָה}}), cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=1|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=41|verse=15}}; even (contrary to {{GHGpar|29|q}}) in a ''closed'' pausal syllable, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=שָׁכֵן}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=33|verse=12}} (out of pause {{GHGheb|text=שָׁכַן}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=32|verse=16}}); but {{GHGheb|text=קָמַ֑ל}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=33|verse=9}}, &c., according to {{GHGpar|29|q}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|44|d}}
2. In some weak stems ''middle a'', the {{GHGterm|Pathaḥ}} under the second radical sometimes, in a closed toneless syllable, becomes {{GHGheb|text=־ִ}}, and, in one example, {{GHGheb|text=־ֶ}}. Thus from {{GHGheb|text=יָרַשׁ}}: {{GHGheb|text=וִיֽרִשְׁתָּהּ|translate=and thou shalt possess it}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=17|verse=14}}; {{GHGheb|text=וִיֽרִשְׁתָּם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=19|verse=1}}; {{GHGheb|text=וִיֽרִשְׁתֶּם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=4|verse=1}}, and frequently; from {{GHGheb|text=יָלַד|translate=to bring forth, to beget}}; {{GHGheb|text=יְלִדְתִּ֫יךָ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=2|verse=7}} (cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=11|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=2|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=15|verse=10|hidebook=1}}); from {{GHGheb|text=פּוּשׁ}}; {{GHGheb|text=וּפִשְׁתֶּם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mal|chapter=3|verse=20}}; from {{GHGheb|text=שָׁאַל}}; {{GHGheb|text=שְׁאִלְתִּיו|translate=I have asked him}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=1|verse=20}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=13|verse=6}}), and three times {{GHGheb|text=שְׁאֶלְתֶּם}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=12|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=5|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=21|verse=29}}. Qimḥi already suggests the explanation, that the ''ĭ'' (''ĕ'') of these forms of {{GHGheb|text=שׁאל}} and {{GHGheb|text=ירשׁ}} is the original vowel, since along with {{GHGheb|text=שָׁאַל}} and {{GHGheb|text=יָרַשׁ}} are also found {{GHGheb|text=שָׁאֵל}} and {{GHGheb|text=יָרֵשׁ}} (see the Lexicon). The possibility of this explanation cannot be denied (especially in the case of {{GHGheb|text=יָרַשׁ}}, see {{GHGpar|69|s}}); the ''ĭ'' in these forms might, however, equally well have arisen from an attenuation of ''ă'' ({{GHGpar|27|s}}), such as must in any case be assumed in the other instances. Moreover, it is worthy of notice that in all the above cases the ''ĭ'' is favoured by the character of the following consonant (a sibilant or dental), and in most of them also by the tendency towards assimilation of the vowels (cf. {{GHGpar|54|k}} and {{GHGpar|64|f}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|44|e}}
3. In verbs ''middle ō'', the {{GHGterm|Ḥolem}} is retained in the tone-syllable, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יָגֹ֫רְתָּ|translate=thou didst tremble}}; {{GHGheb|text=יָכֹ֫לוּ}} in {{GHGterm|pause}} for {{GHGheb|text=יָֽכְלוּ|translate=they were able}}; but in a toneless closed syllable the original short vowel appears in the form of a ''Qameṣ haṭuph''; {{GHGheb|text=יְכָלְתִּ֫יו|translate=I have prevailed against him}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=13|verse=5}}; {{GHGheb|text=וְיָֽכָלְתָּ֫}} (see {{GHGpar|49|h}}) ''then shalt thou be able'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=18|verse=23}}; in a toneless open syllable it becomes vocal {{GHGterm|Š<sup>e</sup>wâ}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=יָֽכְלָה}}, {{GHGheb|text=יָֽכְלוּ}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|44|f}}
